newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan says Taleban accept Uzbek foe's terms.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan says Taleban accept Uzbek foe's terms.

text.p: Pakistan said on Thursday that Afghanistan's Taleban had accepted peace proposals made by northern opposition leader General Abdul Malik, who handed the Islamic militia a stinging defeat in the north last week.

A Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesman told a weekly news briefing that Malik had given the Taleban three conditions for a peace deal, which he passed to the Pakistani consul-general in the northern capital of Mazar-i-Sharif.

Malik had demanded that the Taleban let northern groups keep "exclusive control" of the north, stop trying to disarm opposition fighters there and agree to an "Islamic dispensation" that Malik would set up in cooperation with the Taleban.
"This message was conveyed to the Taleban shura (council) and (its Kandahar-based chief) Mullah Mohammad Omar and they agreed to all these basic principles," the spokesman said.
Pakistan conveyed the Taleban response to Malik on Saturday, the spokesman said, adding: "A reply is expected any time."
Taleban and opposition leaders could not immediately be contacted for comment on the Pakistani account.

It was not clear if Malik had consulted another powerful foe of the Taleban, former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, whose ethnic Tajik fighters are battling the Islamic militia north of Kabul, before making his peace overture.

If confirmed, the Taleban's agreement to Malik's proposals would mark a drastic policy change for the Islamic militia, which has hitherto shown implacable determination to force all opposition factions to bend to its will and surrender.

Malik defected to the Taleban last month in a mutiny against former opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum, but switched sides again after Taleban fighters entered Mazar-i-Sharif and began enforcing their strict Islamic code.
Malik's ethnic Uzbek troops linked up with Shi'ite Moslem militiamen to drive the Taleban out of the city in street battles that cost the Taleban an estimated 300 dead.

The Pakistani spokesman denied Afghan opposition charges that Pakistan was helping the Taleban, saying Islamabad had evidence of "external support for the (anti-Taleban) minority factions", which he said were receiving "planeloads of supplies".
He refused to specify which country or countries were aiding the Taleban's foes. "That I leave for you to guess," he said.
The Taleban have in the past accused Iran, Russia and Uzbekistan of supporting opposition factions.
The spokesman defended Pakistan's action in becoming the first country to recognise the Taleban government on May 25, a day after the Islamic militia entered Mazar-i-Sharif.

He said Pakistan had delayed recognition until the mainly ethnic Pashtun Taleban reached out to other ethnic and political groups, which he said seemed to have happened when the militia forged its short-lived understanding with Malik's forces.
The spokesman said Pakistan would not withdraw its recognition despite the Taleban's defeat. "But we will continue to encourage them to reach out to other groups," he added.
